entries.seminar_title: When Decentralization Works: Leadership Quality and Student Achievement
entries.speaker: C. Kirabo Jackson
entries.abstract: This paper studies when decentralization improves public service delivery. I analyze a Chicago reform that awarded select principals greater autonomy over budgets and operations while holding resources largely unchanged. A meta-analysis of similar reforms shows substantial heterogeneity, including both positive and negative effects. Building on insights from public finance, contract design, and psychology, I argue that the returns to autonomy depend on the capacity of local decision-makers (i.e., principals in this context) and the alignment of their objectives with those of central authorities. Event-study estimates show that, on average, increased autonomy improved achievement by about 0.1 standard deviations, effects comparable to resource-intensive interventions but achieved at minimal cost. However, deconvolution analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity, with both negative and positive effects. Design-based evidence supports the theoretical predictions; high-performing principals benefit more, reallocating resources effectively (e.g., reducing class sizes), and schools with atypical student populations benefit more and may tailor services to local needs. These results highlight that local capacity, aligned incentives, and heterogeneity are central to the success of decentralization reforms.
entries.bio: Abraham Harris Professor of Education and Social Policy

entries.seminar_title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
entries.speaker: Evan Munro
entries.abstract: We study the optimal design and analysis of experiments for estimating spillover effects. Assuming a known (e.g., linear) exposure mapping, we characterize the treatment-assignment distribution and regression-based estimator that minimize worst-case asymptotic variance against a broad class of distributions of unobservables. The design problem yields an intuitive solution in which the planner trades off spillover signal strength against dispersion of spillover variation. The analysis problem yields a simple recentered instrumental variable estimator to best leverage this variation. This framework produces natural solutions in several benchmark cases—such as clustered exposure—and suggests computationally tractable approximations for general networks, including bipartite settings. We illustrate these new tools in semi-synthetic experiments based on three applications from development economics. Our approach yields large standard error reductions in both experiments, increasing effective sample sizes by 50–100% or more.
entries.bio: Assistant Professor of Econometrics and Statistics

entries.seminar_title: Knowing the Numbers: Performance Data and Microenterprise Outcomes in Uganda
entries.speaker: Emma Riley
entries.abstract: Can increasing business owners’ knowledge of their enterprise performance improve firm outcomes? We explore this question through a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 623 female-owned retail businesses in Kampala, Uganda. At baseline, 82% of owners under-estimate their sales, by 46% on average. Firms were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) control, (2) record-keeping encouragement, or (3) the same record-keeping plus fortnightly business analytics (the ``Performance Summary'') —simple summaries of key business metrics over time. We find that receiving the Performance Summary leads to a 36% (USD 332 PPP) increase in inventory spending, a 39% (USD 448 PPP) increase in sales and a 22% (USD 52 PPP) increase in profits compared to the control group. The Performance Summary also reduces owners' under-estimate of their sales, and the effects are concentrated among the owners who under-estimated their sales at baseline. In contrast, encouraging record-keeping alone has no measurable effect, which suggests that the gains come from the summary of the records and not from the collection of the data.

entries.speaker: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
entries.abstract: We study the macroeconomic impact of route-specific shipping disruptions on the U.S. economy and their implications for trade policy. Using high-frequency satellite data on the universe of U.S.-bound container vessels between 2016 and 2025, we construct novel measures of potential and effective shipping capacity that account for disruptions arising from port congestion, Suez and Panama Canal bottlenecks, slow steaming, and vessel rerouting. These measures allow us to document new facts about the evolution of U.S.-bound shipping capacity, the sources of capacity losses, and changes in shipping efficiency. We develop a multi-route general equilibrium model to quantify the impact of shipping disruptions. The 2021 West Coast port congestion during the COVID-19 pandemic reduced welfare by 0.9% of GDP, while the security threats from the 2023–2024 Houthi attacks led to a welfare loss of 0.4% of GDP. The U.S. Navy's intervention in the Red Sea helped contain the effect of these attacks, yielding a benefit of 0.2% of GDP at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs, by alleviating route congestion, can mitigate or even reverse the standard inflationary effect, although the effect on welfare depends on the degree of retailers' market power.

entries.seminar_title: Piece by Piece, Hour by Hour: Incentives, Productivity, and Turnover.
entries.speaker: Jared Grogan
entries.abstract: The choice of compensation method can affect employees’ effort levels, their selection into employment, and their human capital accumulation at a particular firm. However, in settings with especially high turnover, the costs of continually replacing employees may be substantial. We analyze a large group of employees paid primarily by piece rates but who are required to perform many tasks besides the one on which incentive payments are made. We explore whether a change in compensation scheme intended to leave mean earnings constant but that adds time-based compensation for the non-primary tasks can affect worker productivity and turnover. We use the staggered adoption of a new incentive contract for long distance truck drivers at a large American truckload motor carrier to perform a quasi-experimental analysis. We estimate effects on driving and non-driving work outcomes as well as the likelihood that drivers will quit over a given period of time. We discuss potential mechanisms behind the reported effects, and the costs and benefits of the compensation change that can be estimated with available data are reported and interpreted.
